title: Single Number
summary: Every value appears twice except one. Return it in O(n) time and O(1) space.

perf.label: n = 29,999
perf.gen: int[] d = BCB.distinct(15000, -30000, 30000); int[] a0 = BCB.repeatEach(Arrays.copyOf(d, 14999), 2, new int[] { d[14999] });

statement:
Every value in `nums` appears exactly twice, except for one value that appears once. Return that value.

Use O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

The extra-space limit rules out counting with a hash map. Think about an operation that cancels a value with itself.
constraints: Every value appears twice except one
hints: A HashSet finds it but uses O(n) space. Which operation cancels a value with itself?
XOR: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, and the order does not matter.
XOR all the values together; the pairs cancel and only the single value remains.
explain: The 2 appears twice and the 1 once, so the answer is 1. XOR-ing all values works because the pair cancels: `2 ^ 2 ^ 1 = 1`.

title: Number of 1 Bits
summary: Return the number of set bits in the binary representation of n (treat negative values as their 32-bit pattern).
statement:
Return the number of `1` bits in the 32-bit binary representation of `n` (its Hamming weight).

Negative inputs are counted by their 32-bit two's-complement pattern, so `-1` has 32 set bits.

For example 128 is `10000000`, a single 1 bit. Count every set bit of the 32-bit pattern, including the sign bit for negative inputs.
hints: Check the lowest bit with n & 1, then shift. Use >>> (unsigned shift) so a negative number does not loop forever.
A faster trick: n & (n − 1) clears the lowest set bit.
Count how many times you can apply it before n becomes 0. (Integer.bitCount is the library answer.)
explain: 11 in binary is `1011`, which has three 1 bits, so the answer is 3.

title: Power of Two
summary: Return whether n is a power of two.
statement:
Return `true` if `n` is a power of two, meaning `n == 2^x` for some integer `x ≥ 0`.

Zero and negative numbers are not powers of two.

For example 16 is 2⁴ and returns `true`, while 6 is not a power of two. A power of two has exactly one 1 bit in binary.
hints: In binary, a power of two has exactly one bit set.
n & (n − 1) clears the lowest set bit. For a power of two, that leaves 0.
So the answer is n > 0 && (n & (n − 1)) == 0. The n > 0 check rules out 0 and −2³¹.
explain: 1 is 2⁰, so it is a power of two and the answer is `true`.

title: Missing Number
summary: nums holds n distinct values from 0..n. Return the one that is missing, in O(1) extra space.
statement:
`nums` contains `n` distinct numbers taken from the range `0` to `n`, so exactly one number of that range is missing. Return it.

Use O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

One way to see it: the sum 0 + 1 + … + n is known, so the missing value is that sum minus the sum of `nums`. XOR gives the same result without any risk of overflow.
hints: You know which numbers should be there: 0, 1, …, n.
The expected sum is n(n + 1) / 2; subtract the actual sum.
XOR avoids any overflow concern: XOR every index 0 … n with every value, and the pairs cancel, leaving the missing number.
explain: There are 3 numbers, so they come from the range 0 to 3. Of 0, 1, 2 and 3, only 2 is missing, so the answer is 2.

title: Counting Bits
summary: Return an array where element i is the number of 1 bits in i, for every i from 0 to n, in O(n).
statement:
Return an array `ans` of length `n + 1` where `ans[i]` is the number of `1` bits in the binary representation of `i`, for every `i` from `0` to `n`.

Aim for O(n) time.

The answer has one entry per number from 0 to `n` inclusive. Each entry can be built from a smaller one, for example `ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`.
hints: Counting the bits of each number from scratch is O(n log n). Reuse earlier answers.
i >> 1 drops the lowest bit, so ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1).
Alternatively ans[i] = ans[i & (i − 1)] + 1, since i & (i − 1) clears one set bit.
explain: For `n = 2`: 0 is `0` (zero 1 bits), 1 is `1` (one), and 2 is `10` (one). So the answer is `[0,1,1]`.

title: Reverse Bits
summary: Reverse the order of the 32 bits of n and return the result (as a signed Java int).
statement:
Reverse the order of the 32 bits of `n`: bit 0 becomes bit 31, bit 1 becomes bit 30, and so on. Return the result as a Java `int`, which means it can come out negative when the new top bit is 1.

Leading zeros count: the input is always treated as exactly 32 bits, so a small number reverses into a large one.
hints: Build the result one bit at a time, 32 times.
Each step: shift the result left by 1, add n & 1, then shift n right with >>>.
Do exactly 32 iterations even if n becomes 0 early, so the bits end up in the right positions.

title: Single Number II
summary: Every value appears three times except one, which appears once. Return it in O(n) time and O(1) space.

perf.label: n = 29,998
perf.gen: int[] d = BCB.distinct(10000, -1000000, 1000000); int[] a0 = BCB.repeatEach(Arrays.copyOf(d, 9999), 3, new int[] { d[9999] });

statement:
Every value in `nums` appears exactly three times, except for one value that appears exactly once. Return that value.

Use O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

XOR alone doesn't work here, because a value appearing three times doesn't cancel. Count how many times each bit is set and take that count modulo 3.
constraints: Every value appears three times except one
hints: XOR no longer cancels: three copies leave one behind. Look at each bit position separately.
For each of the 32 bit positions, count how many values have that bit set. Taken modulo 3, the count is that bit of the single value.
A constant-space alternative tracks "seen once" and "seen twice" bit masks: ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos; twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones.
explain: 2 appears three times and 3 appears once, so the answer is 3. Counting each bit position modulo 3 keeps only the bits of the value that appears once.

title: Sum of Two Integers
summary: Return a + b without using the + or − operators.
statement:
Return the sum of the integers `a` and `b` without using the `+` or `-` operators anywhere in your solution.

This is a bit-manipulation exercise: think about how a computer adds two numbers in binary.
hints: Think of binary addition by hand: each column produces a sum bit and maybe a carry.
a ^ b adds the bits without carrying; (a & b) << 1 gives the carries.
Repeat with a = a ^ b and b = carry until there is no carry left. Two's complement makes negative numbers work too.
explain: 1 is `01` and 2 is `10`. Their XOR is `11` (the sum without carries) and their AND shifted left is `00` (no carries), so the result is 3.

title: Single Number III
summary: Exactly two values appear once and all others appear twice. Return the two singles in any order, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

perf.label: n = 30,000
perf.gen: int[] d = BCB.distinct(15001, -1000000, 1000000); int[] a0 = BCB.repeatEach(Arrays.copyOf(d, 14999), 2, new int[] { d[14999], d[15000] });

statement:
In `nums`, exactly two values appear once and every other value appears exactly twice. Return the two values that appear once, in any order.

Use O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

The two single values differ in at least one bit. Using that bit to split `nums` into two groups puts one single value in each group, and each group can then be XOR-ed on its own.
constraints: Exactly two values appear once; all others appear twice
hints: XOR of everything gives a ^ b, where a and b are the two singles. Since a ≠ b, some bit of a ^ b is 1.
Pick one such bit (x & −x gives the lowest set bit). a and b differ in it.
Split all values into two groups by that bit and XOR each group: pairs still cancel, and each group leaves one single. Use long or care with −2³¹ when taking the lowest bit.
explain: 1 and 2 each appear twice; 3 and 5 appear once. XOR of everything is `3 ^ 5 = 6` (`110`); splitting the values by its lowest set bit separates 3 from 5. So the answer is `[3,5]`, in either order.

title: Add Binary
summary: a and b are binary numbers written as strings. Return their sum as a binary string.
statement: `a` and `b` are binary numbers written as strings of `0`s and `1`s. Return their sum, also as a binary string.
constraints: Neither has leading zeros, except "0" itself
hints: With up to 10⁴ bits, converting to an int or long overflows. Add digit by digit instead.
Walk both strings from the right with a carry, like grade-school addition in base 2.
Each step: sum = bitA + bitB + carry; write sum % 2 and carry sum / 2. Keep going while either string has digits or the carry is 1, then reverse.
explain: 11 in binary is 3 and 1 is 1, so the sum is 4, which is "100" in binary.

title: Bitwise AND of Numbers Range
summary: Return the bitwise AND of every integer from left to right, inclusive.
statement: Given two integers `left` and `right` that describe the range `[left, right]`, return the bitwise AND of **every** integer in that range, including both ends.
hints: ANDing every number one by one can take about 2 · 10⁹ steps.
If a bit position changes anywhere between left and right, some number in the range has a 0 there, so that bit is 0 in the answer.
The answer is the common binary prefix of left and right, followed by zeros. Shift both right until they are equal, then shift back.
explain: 5 = 101, 6 = 110 and 7 = 111. Only the top bit is set in all three, so the AND is 100 in binary, which is 4.

title: Minimum Array End
summary: Build a strictly increasing array of n positive integers whose bitwise AND equals x. Return the smallest possible value of the last element.
statement: Construct an array `nums` of `n` positive integers that is **strictly increasing** and whose bitwise AND of all elements equals `x`. Return the minimum possible value of `nums[n − 1]`.
hints: Every element must contain all the 1-bits of x, so nums[0] = x is the best start.
The bits that are 0 in x are free. The k-th valid number (counting from 0) is x with the binary digits of k written into those free positions, lowest first.
So the answer is x with the bits of n − 1 placed into x's zero bits. The result can exceed 2³¹: use a 64-bit value.
explain: With x = 4 (100), each element must keep that bit. The smallest three such numbers are 4 (100), 5 (101) and 6 (110), so the last element is 6.
